newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan foes battle for heights north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghan foes battle for heights north of Kabul.

text.p: Rival Afghan militia pounded each other with artillery, mortar and rocket fire on Wednesday, vying for heights overlooking one of two roads leading into Taleban- held Kabul, witnesses and rival commanders said.

Forces of the ousted Burhanuddin Rabbani government said they launched a major assault to capture the De Sabz pass leading into northeast Kabul, towards which they have been moving back after pulling out last month when the Taleban attacked.

"We are progressing. We have taken control of the high positions (on De Sabz pass) and we will soon clear the Taleban's remaining positions," Mehrabodin Masstan, spokesman for ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, told reporters behind Masood lines.
He said the forces of northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, which joined Masood's front-line last week, had taken part in the attack.
However, by late-afternoon there were no signs of a major advance by Masood or Dostum on the eastern side of the plain girded by craggy hills leading to Kabul.
Taleban fighters some 25 km (16 miles) north of the city were relaxed and watching Masood mortar fire landing on their side's positions a couple of kilometres (one mile) away.

On the other front, on the main road running near the west side of the plain, it was even quieter as the two sides shelled each other's positions around a series of hills running across the plain, Reuters correspondents reported.
Taleban fighters denied they had been pushed out of hilltop positions and said they were trying to oust Masood's forces from hills in the middle of the plain.
Three artillery pieces fired salvoes at the position and others on the plains behind, sending columns of smoke rising from the hilltop, wedged between ridges the Taleban said they controlled.
One of the hilltops a mile (less than a kilometre) to the east was coming under mortar fire, one Taleban fighter said. Travellers reported some Taleban casualties had been ferried to Kabul.
There was no immediate response on the ground to calls for a ceasefire, including one on Tuesday by the United Nations Security Council.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali also said a multilateral presence was needed in Kabul if any ceasefire was reached.
The latest initiative, by neighbour Pakistan, was awaiting a response on Wednesday from Dostum.
Masood forces, whose advance has stalled for the past week some 30 minutes' drive north of the capital, appear determined to take remaining ground held by the Taleban.
Reuters correspondent Chris Bird quoted commanders as saying they now held positions overlooking the De Sabz pass and near Khair Khana, a pass descending into northern Kabul.
But correspondents using the road through Khair Khana on Wednesday morning saw little change on the ground.

Bird reported heavily shelling by Masood forces just before dawn. Then, a rare four-hour lull set in before Taleban artillery and mortars opened up on Masood's positions on and around the main road north from Kabul.

Taleban fighters said their target was to retake Bagram airbase, 50 km (30 miles) north of the capital, in a push up the so-called new road which runs on the eastern side of the plain parallel to the main route.
Masood, bolstered by the alliance with Dostum and his tanks and artillery and men, has called for the demilitarisation of Kabul, ravaged by four years of factional fighting.
But Taleban leader Mullah Mohammad Omar told the Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) his movement would defend the capital.
"We will strongly defend Kabul," he said of the city the Taleban captured on September 27 and imposed Islam's stern Sharia law on it.

Taleban, wearing their trademark black turbans and driving around in the only modern vehicles -- apart from those used by western aid workers -- to be seen in the capital, were still numerous on Wednesday.
Taleban fighters on the front-line said they had heard all the talk about a ceasefire. "But they don't want to stop fighting," said one with a nod towards Masood's positions.

"We'll go on fighting, too and we'll push them back to where they came from," he added in a reference to Masood's Panjsher Valley stronghold in the Hindu Kush from which he counter-attacked 10 days ago.
